reason: The sources corroborate over a dozen atomic facts across seven distinct sites detailing Mariner 1's launch failure, the missing overbar bug, and Mariner 2's subsequent success.
story: On July 22, 1962, NASA launched Mariner 1 toward Venus aboard an Atlas-Agena rocket, aiming for humanity's first planetary flyby. Less than five minutes into the flight, the rocket began fishtailing erratically. Heading dangerously toward Atlantic shipping lanes, it was blown apart by the range safety officer at 293 seconds, just six seconds before booster separation. The culprit became legendary when Arthur C. Clarke dubbed it the most expensive hyphen in history. But it was not actually a hyphen. Transcribers copying handwritten flight equations into computer code had omitted a single mathematical overbar above the letter R. That overbar instructed the ground computer to smooth out noisy radar data. When an onboard beacon briefly glitched, the guidance software mistook minor jitter for extreme velocity changes, sending violent corrections that wrecked the flight. Fortunately, NASA launched identical twin Mariner 2 five weeks later with corrected code, making history at Venus.
angle: NASA's first planetary mission was blown out of the sky because a transcriber forgot to draw a single horizontal bar over the letter R in handwritten guidance math.

claims.claim: Mariner 1 was designed to conduct the first American planetary flyby of Venus.
Mariner 1 launched from Cape Canaveral on an Atlas-Agena rocket on July 22, 1962.
During ascent, the rocket began veering off course toward Atlantic shipping lanes.
A range safety officer sent a destruct command, blowing the rocket apart in flight.
The self-destruct order was issued approximately 293 seconds after liftoff, less than five minutes into the flight.
The destruct command was sent roughly six seconds before the Agena upper stage was scheduled to separate, after which destruction would no longer be possible.
Popular press accounts and Arthur C. Clarke famously dubbed the missing symbol the most expensive hyphen in history.
The missing symbol was not a hyphen, but a mathematical overbar written above the letter R.
The overbar functioned as a smoothing operator instructing the computer to average tracking data over time instead of reacting to raw radar readings.
Without the smoothing bar, the guidance software treated minor signal noise as wild velocity fluctuations and issued erroneous steering corrections.
The failure was a compound fault requiring both the software omission and an in-flight hardware radar tracking failure to trigger.
The identical flawed guidance code had previously flown on Ranger lunar missions without failing because the hardware tracking beacon had not glitched.
Mariner 1 carried scientific instruments to probe Venus's atmosphere and magnetic field, but did not carry a visual camera.
The loss of Mariner 1 represented an 18.5 million dollar setback for NASA in 1962 dollars.
NASA launched the identical backup probe Mariner 2 about five weeks later on August 27, 1962.
Mariner 2 successfully flew past Venus on December 14, 1962, becoming the first spacecraft to fly by another planet and transmit data.

disputed: Hyphen vs. Overbar: Popular media and Arthur C. Clarke claimed a missing hyphen caused the explosion, but technical investigations proved it was a missing mathematical overbar over the letter R denoting a smoothed value; scripts should present the hyphen label as a popular misnomer.
Destruct timing: S2 states T+294.5 seconds, while S3, S5, S6, and S7 state 293 seconds; scripts should round to approximately 293 seconds or under five minutes.

Necessity of destruction: Program director Jack James believed destroying the rocket was unnecessary because it would have fallen harmlessly in the open ocean; scripts should attribute this claim specifically to James.
